model: claude-opus-5-5 (Claude Code general-purpose subagent, instructions in the task prompt)
opening: Teach me how percentage gains and losses work on investments, properly.

turns.text:
Let's do this properly. Here's how I've broken the topic into subskills:

1. Calculating a percentage gain or loss from start and end values
2. Gain/loss asymmetry (why a 50% loss needs more than a 50% gain to recover)
3. Compounding sequential returns (multiplying, not adding)
4. Average return vs. actual return (arithmetic vs. geometric mean, volatility drag)
5. Annualizing returns (CAGR over multi-year periods)
6. Percent vs. percentage points (and relative vs. absolute changes)

I'll start by asking a few questions, one at a time, to see what you already know. I won't teach anything until we're done with these. Just answer as best you can. "I don't know" is a perfectly useful answer.

Question 1: A stock goes from $80 to $100. What's the percentage gain? Then it falls from $100 back to $80. What's the percentage loss? Show how you got each number.
The gain is $20 on $80, so 20 divided by 80 is 25%. Then it drops the same $20 back down, so that's a 25% loss, which makes sense since you end up right where you started.

Got it, I've noted your answer and your reasoning. I'm not going to say yet whether it's right. We'll come back to it once the diagnostic is done.

Question 2: You invest $1,000. In year one it gains 10%, and in year two it loses 10%. How much money do you have at the end of year two, and what's your total percentage gain or loss over the two years?
You'd have $1,000 at the end, so 0% total. The 10% gain and the 10% loss just cancel each other out.

Noted. As before, I'll hold off on saying whether that's right until the diagnostic is finished.

Question 3: Over three years, a fund returns +50%, then -50%, then +50%. A friend says, "The average annual return is about 16.7%, so the fund grew about 16.7% per year." What does $1,000 invested at the start actually end up as, and is your friend's claim reasonable? Explain your reasoning.
The first +50% and -50% cancel out, so you're back at $1,000, then the last +50% takes you to $1,500. That's 50% total over three years, so about 16.7% a year sounds pretty reasonable to me.

Noted. I'll come back to this one too once the diagnostic is done.

Question 4: Your savings account's interest rate goes from 2% to 3%. Your bank's ad says "rates up 1%!" and a news headline says "rates up 50%!" Which one is right, and why?
I'd say the bank is right, it went from 2% to 3% so that's up 1%. The 50% headline sounds like clickbait to me.

Noted. That's the diagnostic done. Here's where I'd place you to start:

    1. Gain/loss from start & end values  [████░░░░░░]  2/5
    2. Gain/loss asymmetry                [██░░░░░░░░]  1/5
    3. Compounding sequential returns     [██░░░░░░░░]  1/5
    4. Average vs. actual return          [░░░░░░░░░░]  0/5
    5. Annualizing returns (CAGR)         [██░░░░░░░░]  1/5
    6. Percent vs. percentage points      [██░░░░░░░░]  1/5

I'm not going to say which answers were right or wrong. You'll work that out yourself as we go, and it'll stick much better that way. I'll say this much: some of your four answers had problems, and they're related. The same idea runs through all of them.

I suggest we start with subskill 1. Everything else depends on it, and your first answer is the best place to dig in. If you'd rather start somewhere else, say so.

Let's go back to Question 1. When you worked out the 25% gain, you divided $20 by $80. When the stock falls from $100 to $80, what value is the stock starting from, and what number should the $20 be divided by?
It's starting from $100 on the way down, so I guess the $20 gets divided by 100? That would make it 20%, not 25%, which feels weird since it's the same $20.

Yes. On the way down it's $20 out of $100, so that's a 20% loss. Your original "25% loss" was wrong. You treated the drop as the mirror image of the gain, and it isn't.

You're right that it feels weird, and that feeling is worth working through, because the rest of the topic depends on it. The dollar amount is the same both times. The only thing that changed is the number you divided by.

So, in your own words: in any percentage gain or loss, what is the percentage *of*? And why does that make the trip up from $80 and the trip back down from $100 come out as different percentages, even though the $20 is the same?

I guess it's a percentage of wherever you start from. Going up you start at $80 so the $20 is a bigger chunk of that, and going down you start at $100 so the same $20 is a smaller chunk. But a 50% drop is still fixed by a 50% gain though, right?

That's the right idea. A percentage is always a percentage of the starting value, so the same $20 is a bigger share of $80 than of $100. I'm not raising your level yet. You got there with my help, and I want to see you apply it on your own later.

On your 50% question, I won't answer it for you. Use the rule you just stated and test it yourself.

You have $100 and it drops 50%. How much do you have now? Then that new amount gains 50%. How much do you end up with?
Okay, $100 drops 50% so that's $50. Then 50% of $50 is $25, so I'd be at $75... wait, that's not back to $100 at all. Huh, so the 50% gain is smaller because it's 50% of a smaller number?

Yes, that's right. The 50% gain is 50% of $50, not 50% of $100, so it only adds $25 and you end up at $75. You've just run into subskill 2, gain/loss asymmetry: after a loss you're starting from a smaller number, so the same percentage gain adds fewer dollars than the loss took away.

You worked that out yourself, which is good. I'm still not changing any levels yet, though. I want to see you use it without me setting up the steps first.

So turn it around. You're at $50 after the 50% drop. What percentage gain do you need to get back to exactly $100? Show how you got it.
